newsitem.title: CHINA: HK warns off currency speculators as stocks tumble.
newsitem.headline: HK warns off currency speculators as stocks tumble.

text.p: Hong Kong vowed on Tuesday it would not be bowed by currency speculators like its regional neighbours, as the local stock market tumbled on exchange rate jitters.
The Hong Kong dollar touched a low of HK$7.7430 in early afternoon versus an opening level of HK$7.400/10, but it ended the day slightly firmer at HK$7.385/95.
Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa said on Tuesday speculators trying to attack the Hong Kong dollar were sure to fail.

"We have such a good foundation. So if speculators want to make any attack on the Hong Kong dollar, they are bound to fail. We're very confident (about it)," he told reporters after a meeting with his cabinet.
"As Asian currencies have been fluctuating and the world's stock markets have been correcting recently, Hong Kong as an international city of course will have ups and downs," he said.
"But as our foundation is so good, that definitely won't have a long-term impact," he said.

Hong Kong's short-term interest rates soared and its stock market plummeted on Tuesday amid fears that the local dollar would come under attack as speculators turned their sights to the last Asian currency still pegged to the U.S. dollar.
Other currencies around the region have been forced from their pegs, effectively devalued, since early July.

The Hong Kong dollar also is one of the most stoutly defended, with local foreign currency reserves of US$82 billion as of June 30. A local newspaper said on Saturday that China was prepared to use US$50 billion of its own reserves to defend the Hong Kong unit.
Dong Tao, economist with Schroder Securities (Asia), said Hong Kong's economic fundamentals were far stronger than countries like Thailand, the earliest victim of speculators.

Additionally, unlike other currencies in the region, the Hong Kong dollar is more properly defined as linked, rather than pegged, to the U.S. dollar because each Hong Kong dollar is backed by an equivalent in U.S. dollars.
Hong Kong's sheer financial muscle also meant attacks on the peg carried a high price tag, especially for hedge funds that are highly leveraged, economists said.
The danger is not with the hedge funds, they said, but with small investors that are spooked by the volatility and opt to move their money offshore to protect assets.
Despite the government's defiance, Hong Kong share prices staged their biggest sell-off since March 1996, with the Hang Seng index closing down 619 points, or 3.85 percent, at 15,477.
"Currencies in the Southeast Asian market are generally weak so it is difficult to see a major rebound in stocks," said Patrick Chia, research director at China Everbright Research.
The surge in overnight interest rates in early trade sparked a selloff in rate-sensitive property and banking stocks.
But by late afternoon, overnight rates had come off the day's highs, broadly quoted at 8.00/10.00 percent compared with 18.00/20.00 percent earlier on Tuesday.
Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said speculators attacked the Hong Kong dollar so as to get into the share market.
"They know the Hong Kong dollar is very sound. They attack it intentionally to push up interest rates so as to keep away small investors to make way for big investors," he said.
"Under such circumstances, I believe Hong Kong stock investors need not be so stupid as to be scared off," he said.
Tung said his government would coordinate with the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the de facto central bank, to closely monitor the exchange rate.
The stock exchange and its regulator, the Securities and Futures Commission, had been monitoring stock market operations, he said.
